 1                                   I. INTRODUCTION

 2   Q.   Please state for the record your name and business address.

 3   A.   My name is Ron Nelson. My business address is 4764 E Sunrise Drive, Unit

 4        #508, Tucson, AZ 85718.

 5   Q.   Have you previously filed testimony in this case?

 6   A.   Yes. I previously filed direct testimony on behalf of Coalition for Clean

 7        Affordable Energy on October 23, 2026.

 8   Q.   What is the purpose of your rebuttal testimony?

 9   A.   My rebuttal testimony responds to the direct testimony of other parties on

10        three issues I addressed in my direct testimony: the recovery of incremental

11        costs caused by large loads under EPE’s line extension policy, the allocation

12        of production costs, and the terms of EPE’s proposed large load tariffs,

13        Original Rate Nos. 50 and 51. On the large load tariffs, I respond to other

14        parties’ recommendations on Commission review of Energy Service

15        Agreements (“ESAs”), eligibility thresholds and aggregation, credit-rating

16        exemptions and parent guarantees, and early-termination damages and the

17        ESA term.

 1                      II. INCREMENTAL COST ALLOCATION

 2   Q.   What are Staff’s positions regarding EPE’s line extension proposal?

 3   A.   Staff Witness Jester describes EPE’s proposal as “some minor wording

 4        changes and the addition of a capacity reservation charge for larger new

 5        loads,” and concludes that it “is a rational approach to ensuring that the

 6        customers requesting significant distribution system investments by EPE

7         cover the costs of their request.” 1

8    Q.   Do you agree that EPE’s line extension proposal ensures large loads

 9        pay the incremental costs they cause?

10   A.   No. My concern is not with what EPE’s proposal covers but with what it

11        omits. Witness Jester’s endorsement is limited, by its terms, to “distribution

12        system investments.” It does not address the shared transmission facilities

13        that would not be built but for a large load, which is the gap I identified in

14        my direct testimony. 2

15                The principles cited by Witness Jester point in the same direction,

16        however, even if the mechanism differs. He recommends that “all new

 3       “proportionate share of costs for shared resources, such as transmission,”3

 4       and that it is “not acceptable” for “transmission headroom [to] be consumed

 6       load customers paying for the incremental shared facilities they require,

 9       with a refund mechanism, is consistent with that principle, but provides

10       stronger protection by recovering those costs up front, before they enter rate

11       base. 6 Under my proposed approach, the large load funds the upgrade it

12       triggers, and receives refunds as its load materializes and other customers

13       use of the facility move its ultimate cost responsibility toward a

14       proportionate share. Unlike an allocation set in advance, it also protects

15       other customers if the load never arrives.

 4                       III. EMBEDDED COST ALLOCATION

 5        a. Production Cost Allocation

 6   Q.   How do other parties address EPE’s proposed approach to production

 7        cost allocation?

 8   A.   New Mexico State University Witness Stephens supports EPE’s method.

 9        US Department of Defense and Federal Executive Agencies Witness Blank

10        would apply the Company’s Average and Excess method, incorporating a

11        four coincident peak component, (“4CP-A&E”) to all production plant,

12        including peaking. Staff Witness Jester, like me, finds that EPE’s method

13        does not reasonably reflect cost causation but recommends deferring any

14        change to EPE’s next rate case.

15   Q.   How do you respond to Witness Stephens?

16   A.   Witness Stephens supports 4CP because EPE is summer-peaking, while




     17

                             Rebuttal Testimony of Ron Nelson

 1          also stating that “a 3 CP allocator, using June, July and August, might be

 2          more appropriate.” 18 His defense of 4CP-A&E rests on 4CP being “more

 3          commonly used,” and both 4 CP and A&E methods being included in the

 4          NARUC Manual. 19 Common use and inclusion in the NARUC Manual,

 5          which is descriptive rather than prescriptive, does not mean that a given

6           methodology is most cost reflective for a given utility’s generation fleet.

7           The NARUC Manual also describes the probability of dispatch (“POD”)

 8          method. 20 POD assigns each unit’s costs to the hours in which it serves load,

 9          so it captures summer-peak cost causation directly rather than through a

10          four-hour proxy.

11   Q.     How do you respond to Witness Blank?

12   A.     Witness Blank frames the question as “whether there is a sufficient cost-

13          causative basis to use different allocators for peaking and other generation,”

14          and concludes there is not. 21 I agree that EPE has not demonstrated that its

 5   A.   I recommend that the Commission adopt a POD approach to production cost

 8   A.   No. Each of them places the burden on Staff and intervenors to identify a

 9   A.   No. A 75 MW threshold would leave many of the large loads EPE is likely

 2            3. Credit Rating Exemptions and Parent Guarantees

 3   Q.   What do other parties recommend regarding EPE’s proposed

 4        exemption from financial security for customers with high credit

 5        ratings?

 6   A.   Witness Mamkhezri does not ask the Commission to change the exemption.

 7        He notes that because the ratings test applies to the entity that signs the ESA,

 8        a special-purpose subsidiary cannot claim the exemption on its parent’s

 9        credit: “That structure is correct and I do not ask the Commission to disturb

10        it.” 52 Witness McGovern supports keeping EPE’s proposed Rate No. 51

11        security provisions, including “security for customers that do not meet

12        specified credit criteria.” 53

13   Q.   Do you agree?

14   A.   I agree with Witness Mamkhezri that a special-purpose subsidiary should

15        not be able to claim the exemption on its parent’s credit. But I continue to

 1        recommend eliminating the exemption. A customer’s credit rating when it

 2        signs an ESA says little about its creditworthiness over a 20-year term, when

 3        ratepayer exposure may be greatest. The exposure security is meant to cover

 4        arises later, if a customer reduces load or exits, and ratings can deteriorate

 5        before then. As I noted in my direct testimony, S&P Global has begun to

 6        flag risks for hyperscale data center customers. 54 A standardized security

 7        based on 36 months of minimum bills is modest relative to the investment

 8        at stake, and it protects ratepayers regardless of how a customer’s credit

 9        changes.

15        specified ratings. 55
